paragraphs: The monastery lay barely three-quarters of a mile outside the town. Alyosha set off along the road at a brisk walk. Nobody else was on it at that hour. Night was nearly down, and it was too dark to make out anything clearly thirty paces ahead. Halfway there the road crossed another. Under a lone willow at the crossing, a figure came into view. The moment Alyosha reached the spot, the figure leapt out and ran at him, yelling savagely:
“Your money or your life!”
“Mitya, it’s you!” cried Alyosha, surprised, though he had been badly frightened.

“Ha ha ha! You weren’t expecting me? I couldn’t decide where to wait for you. Outside her house? Three roads lead away from it, and I might have missed you. So finally I thought, I’ll wait here. You have to pass this spot, there’s no other way to the monastery. Come on, tell me the truth. Crush me like a beetle. But what’s wrong?”

“Nothing, brother—you just scared me. Oh, Dmitri! Father’s blood, only a little while ago.” (Alyosha started to cry. He had been on the edge of tears for a long time, and now something in his soul seemed to snap.) “You nearly killed him—you cursed him—and now, here, you’re joking—‘Your money or your life!’”
“Well, so what? It’s not proper—is that what you mean? Doesn’t suit a man in my position?”
“No—it’s only that—”

“Hold on. Look at the night. See how dark it is, the clouds, the wind that’s picked up. I was hiding under that willow, waiting for you. And I swear by God above, I suddenly thought: why drag on in misery any longer? What is there left to wait for? Here’s a willow, here’s a handkerchief, here’s a shirt. In a minute I can twist them into a rope, and I have my suspenders too. Why go on weighing down the earth and shaming it with my filthy presence? And then I heard you coming—heavens, it was as if something had suddenly flown down to me. So there is someone I love after all! Here he is, my dear little brother, the one I love more than anyone in the world, the only one I love in the world. And at that moment I loved you so much, so much, that I thought, ‘I’ll throw myself on his neck this instant.’ Then a stupid notion came over me: play a joke on you, give you a scare. So I shouted that idiotic ‘Your money!’ Forgive the clowning—it was nonsense, and there’s nothing improper in my soul.... Damn it all, tell me what happened. What did she say? Hit me, crush me, show me no mercy! Was she furious?”
“No, not that.... Nothing like that happened, Mitya. It was—I found the two of them there together.”
“The two of them? Who?”
“Grushenka was at Katerina Ivanovna’s.”
Dmitri was struck speechless.
“Impossible!” he cried. “You’re raving! Grushenka with her?”

Alyosha told him everything that had happened, starting from the moment he walked into Katerina Ivanovna’s. The telling took ten minutes. It couldn’t be called a smooth or orderly account, but he seemed to get it across. He left out no word or deed that mattered, and he often described his own feelings vividly in a single word. Dmitri listened without a sound, fixing him with a terrible stare. Still, Alyosha could see that he understood everything and had caught every point. But as the story went on, his face turned from gloomy to menacing. He scowled and ground his teeth, and his stare grew more rigid, more intense, more terrible. Then, suddenly, and with astonishing speed, that angry, savage face changed. His tight lips came apart, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch burst out laughing, helplessly and without any plan to. He positively shook with it. For a long while he could not say a word.

“So she wouldn’t kiss her hand! She didn’t kiss it—she ran off!” he kept crying out in hysterical glee. It might have been called insolent glee, if it hadn’t burst out so naturally. “And the other one called her a tigress! A tigress she is! So she should be flogged on a scaffold? Yes, yes, she should. That’s exactly my opinion. She should have been long ago. Here’s how it is, brother: let her be punished, but first I have to get well. I know the queen of impudence. That’s her all over! You saw the whole of her in that hand-kissing, the she-devil! In her own line she’s magnificent! So she ran home? I’ll go—ah—I’ll run to her! Alyosha, don’t blame me. I agree, hanging’s too good for her.”
“But what about Katerina Ivanovna!” cried Alyosha sadly.

“I see through her too! I see her as I never have before! It’s a real discovery, like the four continents of the world, I mean the five! What a thing to do! That’s Katya for you, who wasn’t afraid to face a rude, coarse officer and risk a deadly insult, all on a generous impulse to save her father! But the pride, the recklessness, the defiance of fate, the boundless defiance! You say the aunt tried to stop her? That aunt is domineering herself, you know. She’s the sister of the general’s widow in Moscow, and she’s even more high and mighty than the widow. But her husband was caught stealing government funds. He lost everything, his estate and all, and the proud wife had to haul down her flag, and she hasn’t flown it since. So she tried to hold Katya back, and Katya wouldn’t hear of it! She thinks she can overcome anything, and that everything will give way before her. She thought she could bewitch Grushenka whenever she liked, and she believed it herself. She acts a part for her own benefit, and whose fault is that? Do you think she kissed Grushenka’s hand first on purpose, with some motive? No, she really was taken with Grushenka. That is, not with Grushenka, but with her own dream, her own delusion—because it was _her_ dream, _her_ delusion! Alyosha, my darling, how did you ever get away from them, those women? Did you hitch up your cassock and run? Ha ha ha!”

“Brother, you don’t seem to have noticed how badly you insulted Katerina Ivanovna by telling Grushenka about that day. And Grushenka threw it in her face just now: that she had gone to gentlemen in secret to sell her beauty! Brother, what insult could be worse than that?”
What troubled Alyosha most was that his brother seemed pleased at Katerina Ivanovna’s humiliation, incredible as that was.
“Bah!” Dmitri scowled fiercely and slapped his forehead. Only now did it sink in, though Alyosha had just told him about the insult and about Katerina Ivanovna’s cry: “Your brother is a scoundrel!”

“Yes, maybe I did tell Grushenka about that ‘fatal day,’ as Katya calls it. Yes, I told her, I remember it now! It was at Mokroe. I was drunk, the gypsies were singing.... But I was sobbing. I was sobbing then, on my knees, praying to Katya’s image, and Grushenka understood. She understood everything then. I remember, she cried herself.... Damn it all! But it’s bound to be like that now.... Then she cried, and now it’s ‘the dagger in the heart’! That’s women for you.”
He lowered his eyes and fell to thinking.

“Yes, I am a scoundrel, an out-and-out scoundrel!” he said suddenly, in a dark voice. “Whether I cried or not makes no difference, I’m a scoundrel! Tell her I accept the name, if that comforts her. There, enough. Good-by. No use talking! It’s no fun. You go your way and I’ll go mine. And I don’t want to see you again, except as a last resort. Good-by, Alexey!”
He gripped Alyosha’s hand warmly. Then, eyes still on the ground and head down, as if wrenching himself away, he strode quickly off toward the town.
Alyosha watched him go. He could not believe that Dmitri would leave so suddenly.

“Wait, Alexey, one more confession, for you alone!” cried Dmitri, wheeling around. “Look at me. Look at me carefully. You see, here, right here—a terrible disgrace is waiting for me.” (As he said “here,” Dmitri pounded his chest with his fist in a strange way, as though the dishonor sat exactly on his chest, at some spot, in a pocket perhaps, or hung from his neck.) “You know me by now, a scoundrel, a confessed scoundrel. But let me tell you this: nothing I’ve ever done, or ever will do, comes near the baseness of the dishonor I carry this very minute on my breast, here, here. It’s going to happen, though I’m perfectly free to stop it. I can stop it or I can see it through, mark that. Well, I’ll tell you: I’m going to see it through. I won’t stop it. I told you everything just now, but not this, because even I hadn’t the brass for it. I can still pull back. If I do, I can give back half of my lost honor tomorrow, the full half. But I won’t pull back. I’ll carry out my base plan, and you can bear witness that I told you beforehand. Darkness and ruin! No need to explain. You’ll learn it in good time. The filthy back alley, and the she-devil. Good-by. Don’t pray for me, I’m not worth it. And there’s no need, no need at all.... I don’t want it! Go!”
And he abruptly turned away, and this time he was gone for good. Alyosha continued toward the monastery.
“What? I’ll never see him again! What is he saying?” he wondered wildly. “But I’ll certainly see him tomorrow. I’ll hunt him up. I’ll make a point of it. What does he mean?”

He skirted the monastery wall and cut through the pine wood to the hermitage. The door was opened for him, although no one was let in at that hour. His heart trembled as he entered Father Zossima’s cell.

“Why, oh why had he left? Why had the elder sent him out into the world? Here there was peace. Here there was holiness. Out there was confusion and darkness, where a man lost his way and went astray at once....”

In the cell he found the novice Porfiry and Father Païssy, who looked in every hour to ask after Father Zossima. Alyosha heard with alarm that the elder was getting worse and worse. Even his usual talk with the brothers could not be held that day. Normally, every evening after the service, the monks crowded into Father Zossima’s cell. There each one confessed aloud the sins of his day, his sinful thoughts and temptations, and even his quarrels, if he had had any. Some confessed on their knees. The elder absolved them, reconciled them, exhorted them, gave penances, blessed them and sent them away. The opponents of “elders” protested against exactly this general “confession.” They claimed it profaned the sacrament of confession and was almost a sacrilege, though in fact it was something quite different. They even told the diocesan authorities that these confessions did no good, and in great part actually led to sin and temptation. Many of the brothers disliked going to the elder. They went against their will, because everyone else went and because they feared being accused of pride and rebellious ideas. People said some of the monks agreed in advance, “I’ll confess that I lost my temper with you this morning, and you back me up,” just to have something to say. Alyosha knew this really did happen at times. He knew, too, that some of the monks bitterly resented the custom of bringing letters from relatives to the elder first, so that he opened and read them before the people they were meant for.

All this was supposed, of course, to be done freely and in good faith, as voluntary submission and healthy guidance. In fact, though, there was sometimes a good deal of insincerity in the practice, and much that was false and forced. Still, the older and more experienced monks stood by their view. They argued: “For those who have come within these walls in sincere search of salvation, such obedience and sacrifice will surely be healthy and of great benefit. Those who find it irksome and grumble are no true monks and were mistaken to enter the monastery—their place is in the world. Even in the temple a man is not safe from sin and the devil. So it was no use paying too much attention to it.”

“He is weaker. A drowsiness has come over him,” Father Païssy whispered to Alyosha, giving him his blessing. “It’s hard to wake him, and he must not be woken. He was awake for five minutes. He sent his blessing to the brothers and asked for their prayers for him tonight. He means to take the sacrament again in the morning. He remembered you, Alexey. He asked if you had gone away, and was told you were in the town. ‘I blessed him for that work,’ he said. ‘His place is there, not here, for a while.’ Those were his words about you. He remembered you with love and with concern. Do you understand what an honor he paid you? But why has he decided that you should spend some time in the world? He must have foreseen something in your destiny! Understand this, Alexey: if you go back into the world, it must be to do the duty your elder has laid on you, and not for vain frivolity and worldly pleasures.”

Father Païssy left. Alyosha had no doubt that Father Zossima was dying, though he might last another day or two. Alyosha made a firm and fervent resolution. Despite his promises to his father, to the Hohlakovs and to Katerina Ivanovna, he would not leave the monastery the next day. He would stay with his elder to the end. His heart glowed with love. He bitterly blamed himself for having forgotten, even for one instant, the man he had left dying in the monastery, the man he honored above anyone in the world. He went into Father Zossima’s bedroom, knelt, and bowed to the ground before the elder. The elder slept calmly and did not stir. His breathing was even and barely audible, and his face was peaceful.

Alyosha went back to the other room, where Father Zossima had received his guests that morning. He took off his boots and lay down on the hard, narrow leather sofa, which he had used as a bed for a long time, bringing only a pillow. As for the mattress his father had shouted about that morning, he had long since forgotten to sleep on it. He took off his cassock and spread it over himself as a cover. But before going to bed he dropped to his knees and prayed for a long time. In his fervent prayer he did not ask God to lighten his darkness. He only thirsted for the joyful feeling that always came to his soul after the praise and worship that made up his evening prayer. That joy always brought him light, untroubled sleep. As he prayed, he suddenly felt in his pocket the little pink note the servant had handed him as he left Katerina Ivanovna’s. He was disturbed, but he finished his prayer. Then, after some hesitation, he opened the envelope. Inside was a letter to him, signed by Lise, the young daughter of Madame Hohlakov, who had laughed at him that morning in front of the elder.

“Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she wrote, “I’m writing to you behind everyone’s back, even mamma’s, and I know how wrong that is. But I can’t go on living without telling you what I feel, because something has sprung up in my heart, and for now nobody but the two of us must know. But how can I say what I so much want to tell you? They say paper doesn’t blush. I assure you that isn’t true. It’s blushing just the way I am now, all over. Dear Alyosha, I love you. I’ve loved you since I was a child, since our days in Moscow, when you were very different from what you are now, and I’ll love you all my life. My heart has chosen you, so that we can join our lives and spend them together until we’re old. On condition, of course, that you leave the monastery. As for our age, we’ll wait until the age the law sets. By then I’ll certainly be quite strong, walking and dancing. There can’t be any doubt of that.

“You see, I’ve thought of everything. There’s just one thing I can’t picture: what you’ll think of me when you read this. I’m always laughing and getting into mischief. This morning I made you angry, but I assure you that before I took up my pen I prayed in front of the Image of the Mother of God, and now I’m praying, and nearly crying.

“My secret is in your hands. When you come tomorrow, I don’t know how I’ll be able to look at you. Ah, Alexey Fyodorovitch, what if I can’t hold myself in, and laugh like a silly when I look at you, the way I did today? You’ll think I’m a nasty girl who’s making fun of you, and you won’t believe my letter. So I beg you, dear one, if you have any pity for me, when you come tomorrow don’t look me straight in the face. If I meet your eyes, I’m sure to burst out laughing, especially with you in that long gown. I go cold all over thinking of it. So when you come, don’t look at me at all for a while. Look at mamma, or out the window....

“Here I’ve written you a love letter. Oh dear, what have I done? Alyosha, don’t despise me. And if I’ve done something horrid and hurt you, forgive me. Now the secret of my reputation, ruined perhaps for ever, is in your hands.
“I’m certainly going to cry today. Good-by until we meet, our _awful_ meeting.—LISE.
“P.S.—Alyosha! You must, must, must come!—LISE.”

Alyosha read the note in amazement. He read it through twice, thought for a moment, and suddenly gave a soft, sweet laugh. He started. The laugh seemed sinful to him. But a minute later he laughed again, just as softly and happily. Slowly he put the note back in its envelope, crossed himself and lay down. The turmoil in his heart was gone at once. “God, have mercy on all of them. Keep all these unhappy, restless souls in Your care and set them on the right path. All ways are Yours. Save them according to Your wisdom. You are love. You will send joy to all!” Alyosha murmured, crossing himself, and fell into a peaceful sleep.
